candidates.title: Learning SAR ship detectors without inheriting AIS annotation blind spots
candidates.gap: AIS-derived omissions may teach the detector to suppress the very vessels satellite monitoring is meant to recover.
candidates.problem: Some SAR training ships have no box because annotations were generated from AIS. Treating every unlabelled location as sea background can therefore create false negatives. This matters to researchers estimating vessels missed by broadcast-based monitoring.
candidates.question: Can annotation-provenance-aware training preserve small-ship recall under structured label omissions better than teacher pseudo-label completion and uncertainty-based negative mining?
candidates.hypothesis: Modelling omission risk by source and apparent size improves recall at a fixed false-positive budget.
candidates.rival: Apparent improvement comes from extra manual labels or scene-domain differences, rather than better treatment of missing annotations.
candidates.boundary: Pseudo-labelling and uncertainty-based suppression of ambiguous negatives are already implemented. The proposed distinction is AIS-dependent, non-random omission and evaluation on independently annotated ships. That distinction is inferred and not verified novel.
candidates.approach: Fit a compact detector with source-specific background weights or a positive–unlabelled objective. Compare matched label budgets, identical teachers and both random and size-dependent deletion of existing boxes. Use natural annotation-source comparisons only when provenance can be reconstructed.
candidates.data: xView3 has automated/manual label provenance and a documented loading route, but its old dataset subpage returns 404 and the current complete download/licence route was not completed. The GFW CC BY 4.0 detection archive is a smaller fallback; its AIS-derived presence labels alone cannot measure recovery of naturally unlabelled ships.
candidates.fallback: Use a fully annotated, licensed subset and controlled label deletion. This supports robustness to specified omissions, not a claim to have recovered actual dark vessels.
candidates.resources: Estimate: 8–12 GB GPU with small chips, 16–32 GB RAM, 20–80 GB for a bounded scene subset and caches. Full xView3 ingestion is excluded. No training speed or peak memory has been measured.

Ordinary detector and teacher pseudo-labels; remove source weights.
Recall versus omission pattern at equal label budget.
B: safe negative mining
Can a learned ambiguous-negative filter avoid confusing ships and clutter? H: It reduces false negatives without a matching rise in coastal false alarms.
Adapt negative-proposal selection with a held-out calibration set.
Uncertainty mining/UA-PMP control; remove omission features.
False-positive/recall trade-off on independently annotated scenes.
C: teacher reliability
Which pseudo-labels should receive training weight? H: Source-group calibration improves useful pseudo-label precision.
Fit a confidence/reliability model on development scenes.
Fixed-confidence teacher and temperature scaling; remove source grouping.
Pseudo-label precision and downstream detector sensitivity.
candidates.primary: Small-ship recall at a development-fixed false-positive rate per square kilometre, only where geospatial scene area is available; otherwise recall at a fixed false positives/chip budget.
candidates.split: Group complete acquisitions/geographies. Reserve manually annotated scenes for disjoint development and locked evaluation; never train on official validation scenes and then report the same scenes as independent validation.
candidates.baseline: Conventional compact Faster R-CNN/RetinaNet; Allen AI xView3 teacher completion; uncertainty-based negative mining as a close modern control, subject to reproducible code/method access.
candidates.ablation: Random versus source/size-dependent omission; provenance loss, negative filtering and calibration separately; equal manual-label budgets and teacher data.
candidates.errors: Bootstrap acquisitions, use three feasible seeds; stratify by box size, AIS/manual provenance, coastal clutter and sensor. Missing AIS status is not a class label.
candidates.negative: Show that the observed omission effect disappears after scene/source controls, or that pseudo-label completion already resolves it.
candidates.next: Secure the xView3 terms and scene/provenance files, then compare existing pseudo-label and UA-PMP controls on a bounded omission experiment.

candidates.title: Keeping nearshore ships when coastline masks are wrong
candidates.gap: Coastal exclusion suppresses clutter but may also erase boats beside piers or uncertain shoreline boundaries.
candidates.problem: Harbours contain bright structures that resemble SAR ships. Aggressive land masks remove false alarms, but a mask that is shifted or too conservative can hide genuine nearshore vessels.
candidates.question: Can a detector learn when to override an unreliable coastline mask while retaining a fixed harbour false-alarm budget?
candidates.hypothesis: A boundary-reliability gate preserves nearshore ship recall under mask errors better than hard exclusion and naive mask fusion.
candidates.rival: Gains are explained by adding coastal examples or loosening a threshold, not by learning mask reliability.
candidates.boundary: Sea–land guidance, filtering, scattering-aware fusion and hard-negative mining already exist. The narrower proposed test is the coupled cost of realistic mask errors and recovering masked ships; it remains an inferred opportunity.
candidates.approach: Train a compact image detector with a mask-reliability branch, and an auxiliary boundary head using existing sea–land masks. Distinguish naturally uncertain boundaries from deliberately shifted/eroded masks; no new expert mask drawing.
candidates.data: HRSID documents 5,604 images, 16,951 ship instances, inshore/outshore labels and 400 pure-background chips. SL-SSDD provides existing masks. Archives, shared acquisition identifiers and imagery reuse terms have not been verified; the repository's code licence is insufficient by itself.
candidates.fallback: Evaluate controlled mask errors on a reusable subset with existing masks. If no reliable shoreline alignment is recoverable, stop this topic rather than calling arbitrary pixel shifts real coastal errors.
candidates.resources: Estimate: compact detector on an occasional 8–12 GB GPU, 16 GB RAM and 5–20 GB storage. A full dual-branch DINO reproduction is not a required training dependency.
members: A: mask reliability
When should a detector override the coastline? H: A reliability gate reduces missed boundary ships.
Learn image/mask conflict features and a gating head.
Image-only and SLA-style hard/soft masking; remove reliability input.
Recall versus coastal false alarms across mask quality.
B: coastal confusers
Can existing background examples improve ship–structure separation? H: A contrastive loss reduces pier-like false detections.
Train a small coastal contrastive detector head.
Standard detection loss and negative mining; remove hard-negative contrast.
Error rates on held-out harbour/background chips.
C: uncertain boundaries
Can mask uncertainty be predicted from existing labels? H: A learned boundary distribution is safer than a fixed-width buffer.
Fit a probabilistic auxiliary boundary model.
Hard mask, dilated buffers and soft mask; remove uncertainty.
Coverage and detection cost near uncertain boundaries.
candidates.primary: Nearshore ship recall at a fixed false positives/background-chip budget; report AP and offshore recall as secondary outcomes.
candidates.split: Group source acquisitions and coastal regions where recoverable. If scene identifiers are missing, audit duplicates and limit claims to image-level benchmark testing; do not claim geographic generalisation.
candidates.baseline: Compact detector; SLA-Net mask-guidance/filtering; S-DINO as the strong recent methodological neighbour, with compute-matched controls if full reproduction is infeasible.
candidates.ablation: Hard/soft/learned mask; shift versus erosion; coastal negatives; same data/backbone/threshold budget. Report clean-mask performance too.
candidates.errors: Acquisition or image-group bootstrap, several seeds; inspect small boats, piers, bridges, islands and mask-distance bands. Simulated mask errors are a separate test set.
candidates.negative: Show that image-only detection is more reliable, or identify the mask-error level beyond which guidance becomes harmful.
candidates.next: Verify imagery terms, source acquisition groups and mask alignment before using coastal-transfer claims.

candidates.title: Using wind metadata without making SAR detection brittle
candidates.area: Multimodal ML — SAR and environmental data
candidates.gap: Environmental inputs can help explain clutter but may be missing, coarse or unreliable at image acquisition time.
candidates.problem: SAR appearance varies with sea conditions. A detector that relies on environmental metadata can fail when the metadata are low-quality, stale or spatially coarse.
candidates.question: Does quality-aware environmental fusion preserve small-ship detection when wind inputs are absent or inaccurate, while retaining gains on trustworthy inputs?
candidates.hypothesis: A learned reliability gate matches image-only robustness under unreliable metadata and improves recall when metadata are useful.
candidates.rival: The model learns location/season shortcuts or gains simply from metadata dropout regularisation.
candidates.boundary: Environmental conditioning is established in wake research, and physical-feature fusion already addresses motion defocus. The latter uses signal-domain features, not weather. The inferred question concerns measured metadata quality and detector sensitivity, not first multimodal fusion.
candidates.approach: Adapt a compact detector using wind/wind-quality channels with learned gating and missing-input indicators. Evaluate real quality strata separately from synthetic lag/noise experiments; phase errors are not simulated by ordinary image blur.
candidates.data: xView3 documents 500 m wind and wind-quality rasters, but a licensed, aligned scene subset is not yet secured. UEIKAP is CC BY 4.0 and lists AIS/image directories; environmental field availability and scene alignment inside its imagery archives remain uninspected.
candidates.fallback: Use xView3 image-only versus quality-channel models on a bounded accessible subset. If quality fields are unavailable, synthetic missingness alone supports a narrower input-robustness study.
candidates.resources: Estimate: 8–12 GB GPU, 16–32 GB RAM and 20–80 GB storage for selected scenes. No raw-complex SAR reconstruction, simulation platform or continuous weather API is required.
members: A: reliability fusion
Can a learned gate recognise harmful metadata? H: It avoids performance loss at low wind quality.
Train gated image/environment fusion.
Image-only, concatenation and metadata dropout; remove quality gate.
Recall conditional on recorded quality and missingness.
B: training under input errors
Which training perturbations transfer? H: Physically bounded missing/lag scenarios outperform unrestricted noise.
Train uncertainty-aware metadata augmentation.
Ordinary augmentation and dropout; remove lag/quality constraints.
Real-quality-stratum transfer versus synthetic-only gains.
C: confidence under environmental shift
Can confidence remain reliable across wind-quality groups? H: Group-aware calibration limits overconfident false alarms.
Fit a small source-only calibration head.
Global temperature scaling; remove quality grouping.
Calibration and threshold-transfer errors across groups.
candidates.primary: Small-ship recall at a fixed scene-area or chip false-positive budget, reported separately for available real wind-quality groups.
candidates.split: Hold out complete acquisitions and, if supported, regions/seasons. Fit metadata transformations and calibration only on training/development scenes.
candidates.baseline: Compact image-only detector, straightforward metadata concatenation, dropout fusion and a gated-fusion modern control; physics-driven defocus fusion is a conceptual neighbour, not a weather baseline.
candidates.ablation: Quality channel, gate and training perturbations separately; missing versus stale versus noisy inputs; image-only lower-dependency control.
candidates.errors: Scene-block bootstrap and repeated seeds; evaluate sea clutter, tiny ships, nearshore scenes and metadata resolution. Report whether recorded quality actually predicts errors.
candidates.negative: Demonstrate no useful environmental signal at the available resolution, or quantify when image-only detection is preferable.
candidates.next: Inspect one licensed xView3 scene with its quality raster; require real quality variation before claiming practical metadata reliability.

candidates.title: Recognising the same ship when image-derived size is unreliable
candidates.gap: Approximate size helps cross-sensor matching but padding, crop bounds and similar-sized vessels can undermine that shortcut.
candidates.problem: TransOSS already uses crop dimensions and ground sampling distance to approximate physical size. Its paper notes that crops are not exact hull boundaries. An identity model may over-trust those approximate measurements.
candidates.question: Can uncertainty-aware size fusion improve cross-modal re-identification under crop/scale error without sacrificing discrimination between similarly sized vessels?
candidates.hypothesis: Reliability-weighted size embeddings are less brittle than deterministic size fusion at a matched visual backbone.
candidates.rival: Size-blind visual features already solve the problem, or the apparent gain comes from easier gallery composition.
candidates.boundary: Physical-size embeddings, modality alignment, scale-invariant features and identity prototypes already exist. The inferred opportunity is a controlled test of unreliable size information and same-size confusers, not adding size or alignment for the first time.
candidates.approach: Reuse released TransOSS features/weights and train a compact uncertainty-aware size fusion head. Check actual TIFF/GSD fields before treating metadata as measurements. Include size-blind and matched-size galleries.
candidates.data: The 82.9 MB HOSS archive was downloaded and parsed. Its main train/query/gallery directories contain 1,063/176/593 images; extra protocol folders duplicate crops. Identity/sequence/frame/modality filename fields and CC BY 4.0 terms were checked. Pixels, TIFF GSD fields and checkpoint loading were not checked. Visual identity labels do not establish MMSI or registry identity.
candidates.fallback: Use crop padding/scale perturbations with explicit synthetic-error claims, and a visual-only model if usable size metadata cannot be reconstructed. Do not equate changed image pixels with a change in true vessel dimensions.
candidates.resources: Estimate: cached features and small heads on CPU; optional 8–12 GB GPU fine-tuning; 2–10 GB including one checkpoint/cache. Reuse weights instead of the authors' multi-GPU pretraining.

candidates.primary: Cross-modal rank-1 retrieval accuracy on a fixed gallery, with mAP and same-size-gallery performance secondary; confidence research additionally reports false-match risk versus coverage.
candidates.split: Preserve identity-disjoint train/development/test groups and keep all crops/protocol copies of an image together. Check sequence overlap; a new geographic claim is unsupported by the present metadata.
candidates.baseline: TransOSS author code/weights, conventional visual embedding plus metric head, and available SDF-Net/MOS feature controls. Heavy generative pretraining is excluded; incomplete code access must be reported.
candidates.ablation: Size-blind/deterministic/uncertain size; crop padding versus resizing; same-size negative sampling; calibration alone. Keep backbone and gallery composition fixed.
candidates.errors: Bootstrap test identities with repeated gallery sampling; report small/large ships, RGB→SAR and SAR→RGB, distractors and similar-sized confusions.
candidates.negative: Show that deterministic size dominates, that size uncertainty offers no benefit, or that reported gains disappear with matched-size confusers.
candidates.next: Decode a few existing TIFFs, verify the size feature route and load a released checkpoint; then reproduce a size-blind versus deterministic-size control.

candidates.title: Avoiding multiple identities for one ship in optical/SAR image streams
candidates.area: Computer vision — online vessel identity clustering
candidates.gap: Online clustering can split one vessel into many identities; merging those fragments risks combining different vessels.
candidates.problem: HOSS-Bench already evaluates online optical/SAR clustering. Its reported TransOSS result creates about 214 clusters for 85 reference identities. This is a documented fragmentation problem, not an unimplemented task.
candidates.question: Can reversible, modality-aware cluster updates reduce identity fragmentation without increasing false merges?
candidates.hypothesis: Keeping multiple modality-specific exemplars and revisable assignments improves clustering at a fixed pairwise false-merge budget.
candidates.rival: Better static embeddings or a retuned clustering threshold explain the improvement; online state adds no value.
candidates.boundary: Online clustering and cross-modal identity prototypes already exist. A new method must beat the published online threshold protocol and embedding-only improvements. HOSS-Bench is a submission; acceptance and full public protocol code were not verified.
candidates.approach: Cache common embeddings, then learn compact cluster-state or merge/split scoring functions using development identities. Compare irrevocable and reversible decisions under identical observation orders.
candidates.data: HOSS archive contents, licence and sequence/frame filename structure were checked. Sequence/frame indices are not verified elapsed timestamps. Existing train/query/gallery counts are documented; no live stream or MMSI-linked truth is supplied.
candidates.fallback: Use controlled arrival orders and sequence-grouped stress tests on the released crops. Conclusions concern benchmark identity consistency, not real-time voyage tracking or fleet-wide unique vessel counts.
candidates.resources: Estimate: CPU cached-embedding clustering with occasional 8–12 GB GPU adaptation; 2–10 GB storage. No continuous satellite feed or satellite purchase is needed.

Irreversible threshold clustering and agglomeration; disable reversal.
Corrected versus newly introduced merges/splits.

Can acceptance adapt to evidence quantity without knowing the true number of vessels? H: Evidence-aware calibration outperforms a fixed threshold.

candidates.primary: B-cubed F1 and fragmentation at a validation-fixed pairwise false-merge ceiling; report ARI, cluster-count error and pairwise precision/recall.
candidates.split: Use disjoint identities for learning/calibration/testing. Keep duplicate protocol crops together, vary arrival order with fixed seeds, and test modality-blocked orders. Never set thresholds using the test identity count.
candidates.baseline: HOSS-Bench nearest-cluster threshold protocol, DINO/TransOSS fixed features and a conventional clustering control; SDF-Net embeddings test whether representation alone explains the result.
candidates.ablation: Multiple exemplars, modality information, reversal and learned acceptance separately. Match embeddings and observation order.
candidates.errors: Identity-block bootstrap over many order seeds; inspect first-observation errors, distractors, single-modality identities and same-size ships. Sequence order experiments are not elapsed-time validation.
candidates.negative: Quantify the embedding/threshold contribution, or show a false-merge cost that makes reversible clustering unsuitable despite lower cluster-count error.
candidates.next: Reproduce the HOSS-Bench protocol or document its exact reimplementation, then confirm fragmentation with cached released features before inventing a new clustering method.

candidates.title: Knowing when a ship wake is usable evidence
candidates.gap: A missing wake may reflect visibility conditions; a nearby wake-like structure may belong to another vessel or to clutter.
candidates.problem: Wake detection can add movement evidence when a hull is small or ambiguous. SAR wake visibility depends on the observation conditions, so wake absence alone is not evidence of a stationary or absent vessel.
candidates.question: Can a learned wake-usability model improve hull detection or wake association under poor visibility compared with ordinary joint hull/wake fusion?
candidates.hypothesis: Visibility-aware fusion limits harmful wake evidence while retaining gains on clearly visible wakes.
candidates.rival: Joint detection with more negative examples is sufficient; the visibility head learns only sensor/dataset shortcuts.
candidates.boundary: Joint hull/wake detection, environmental wake modelling and synthetic wake generation are established. The narrower inferred question concerns reliability when wake cues are absent, misleading or assigned to the wrong nearby ship.
candidates.approach: Train a compact hull/wake model and a learned usability/association head using existing labels. Keep directly annotated wake presence separate from physical wake generation; do not invent absent-wake truth.
candidates.data: UEIKAP's CC BY 4.0 licence, README and manifests were checked. SAR and optical archives are about 1.57 GB and 11.96 GB; AIS directories exist. Imagery labels, negative coverage, vessel linking and reproducible splits were not parsed. Optical TIFFs are listed as a placeholder; modalities are not assumed simultaneous pairs.
candidates.fallback: Start with the SAR archive and existing labels only. If representative no-wake/background examples are absent, restrict the endpoint to labelled-wake delineation under observed quality, or stop the reliability claim.
candidates.resources: Estimate: 8–12 GB GPU, 16 GB RAM and 10–40 GB storage including extracted subset/caches. No new sea trials or hydrodynamic simulation is necessary.

B: wake-to-ship association

candidates.primary: Hull recall at fixed false alarms and wake-mask F1/IoU on annotated images; wake association accuracy only if the released labels provide links and adequate negatives.
candidates.split: Group acquisition, sensor and vessel/sequence when IDs permit. Prevent nearby chips and repeated observations crossing splits; test SAR/optical separately before any cross-modal claim.
candidates.baseline: Hull-only compact detector; ordinary joint ship/wake model; published lightweight joint detection and visibility-regression approaches as close controls.
candidates.ablation: Usability gate, association and calibration separately; real quality groups versus artificial corruption; matched negative coverage.
candidates.errors: Acquisition-block intervals; analyse low contrast, sea clutter, overlapping wakes, stationary-looking hulls and incorrectly linked wake axes.
candidates.negative: Show that wake cues cannot reliably help on this corpus, or that annotation/negative coverage cannot support absence-based reasoning.

candidates.title: Estimating vessel length when AIS size labels may be wrong
candidates.gap: Regression can reproduce incorrect AIS dimensions or confuse radar distortion with true physical size.
candidates.problem: AIS-reported length is a convenient training target but is not guaranteed correct. SAR motion defocus changes visible extent, creating a second explanation for size-estimation error.
candidates.question: Can robust length regression identify sensitivity to corrupted AIS size labels while separating that effect from observable image degradation?
candidates.hypothesis: A robust heteroscedastic model reduces error under specified label-corruption patterns better than ordinary regression.
candidates.rival: Clipping extreme labels or using a robust loss is sufficient; the uncertainty output does not identify actual incorrect AIS reports.
candidates.boundary: Satellite length estimation and physical defocus compensation already exist. The proposed contribution concerns label reliability, not first length prediction. Without independent dimensions, natural AIS label errors and true physical accuracy cannot be verified.
candidates.approach: Train a compact crop regressor with robust losses and label-uncertainty modelling. Separate known synthetic target corruption from natural target disagreement. Avoid claiming to identify bad reports solely because they disagree with a model trained on the same reports.
candidates.data: GFW CC BY 4.0 presence/length data and manifests were checked in the earlier audit. AIS lengths remain the target, not an independent reference. No adequately sized existing independent registry/manual length set has been secured.
candidates.fallback: Conduct a controlled corruption study on a high-consistency subset and report agreement with its reference labels. This narrows the claim; it does not prove more accurate physical vessel measurement.
candidates.resources: Estimate: cached crop features, CPU regressors or an occasional 8 GB GPU; 5–20 GB storage. Raw SAR phase reconstruction is outside scope.

candidates.title: Separating fishing-vessel classification from local fleet shortcuts
candidates.gap: Size errors and local fleet composition may jointly change a context-based fishing-vessel classifier's decisions.
candidates.problem: Published satellite activity models combine estimated length with environmental context. Service and recreational vessels can resemble fishing vessels in these features, especially when the local vessel mix changes.
candidates.question: How do size-estimation error and local class-composition shift interact, and can a reliability-aware classifier avoid compounding their effects?
candidates.hypothesis: Separating uncertain size evidence from local class priors improves type classification under joint shifts.
candidates.rival: Existing class-prior correction already handles the effect, or apparent gains reflect AIS-label selection rather than classification robustness.
candidates.boundary: The GFW work already uses spatially buffered splits, ensembles and class-prior sensitivity tests. Geography splits or priors alone are not new. The proposed interaction study is inferred; the other two sources are adjacent label/selection evidence, not direct methodological predecessors.
candidates.approach: Train compact feature classifiers with uncertain-size inputs and explicit prior correction. Compare naturally observed regional mixes with controlled reweighting, and keep predicted size versus reference-reported size separate.
candidates.data: Official CC BY 4.0 feature/label releases were checked; context feature archive is about 18.5 GB. The model uses context and estimated length, not necessarily hull imagery. Independent vessel-type labels for unmatched ships are not secured; AIS-labelled transfer is the presently defensible endpoint.
candidates.fallback: Use a cached region/feature subset and restrict findings to vessels with existing type labels. Do not extrapolate classification accuracy to untracked vessels without reference labels.
candidates.resources: Estimate: 32 GB RAM for selected feature extraction, CPU tree/MLP models or occasional 8 GB GPU; 30–80 GB including one archive/subset. No global image ingestion.

candidates.title: Distinguishing sustained vessel co-location from chance satellite crossings
candidates.gap: A single close pair of vessels cannot establish a sustained encounter; revisit cadence changes the apparent evidence.
candidates.problem: Satellite encounter studies already detect nearby or side-by-side ships. A snapshot can also show ordinary navigation or anchoring, while sparse revisit times hide the duration of any co-location.
candidates.question: Can a cadence-aware model distinguish sustained co-location from transient proximity better than snapshot distance rules under explicitly sampled observation gaps?
candidates.hypothesis: A temporal evidence model using observation intervals improves sustained-proximity classification at a fixed false-positive budget.
candidates.rival: Improvements come from AIS-derived duration leakage, or the satellite sampling is too sparse for any model to recover duration.
candidates.boundary: Ship-to-ship activity detection is established. MOSA explicitly reports limited revisit and scarce event truth. The narrower proposal studies observability of sustained proximity; it cannot label cargo transfer or illegality without independent event evidence.
candidates.approach: Train a compact temporal model on existing AIS-derived proximity intervals, then downsample to satellite-like times. Hold out complete encounters/vessel pairs and contrast crossings/anchoring where existing metadata allow. Treat satellite-image pair detection as a separate appearance test.
candidates.data: A free, licensed corpus pairing repeated satellite images with independent encounter-duration labels has not been secured. Published commercial imagery cases and AIS-derived event labels are not such a corpus. GFW analysis and UEIKAP provide adjacent data, not verified transfer events.
candidates.fallback: Use an existing open AIS track subset for controlled cadence experiments. This supports reconstruction of AIS-defined sustained proximity only; it is an AIS-method study until satellite pairing is independently available.
candidates.resources: Estimate: CPU temporal models, 16 GB RAM and 5–30 GB for selected tracks/features; optional frozen image features. Commercial satellite purchases are excluded.

candidates.title: Updating AIS-gap anomaly models when reception coverage changes
candidates.area: Time-series ML — AIS reception and satellite corroboration
candidates.gap: An outdated reception model can make ordinary coverage loss look like unusual vessel behaviour.
candidates.problem: GFW documentation states that reception-quality estimates use 2017–2019 data pending automated updates. Later changes in reception can therefore affect the interpretation of AIS reporting gaps.
candidates.question: Can a compact time-adaptive reception model reduce false gap anomalies under receiver-coverage drift compared with static reception filters?
candidates.hypothesis: Updating background reception estimates from other vessels improves later-period reception prediction and gap-score reliability.
candidates.rival: Changing traffic/transmission behaviour explains the apparent drift; a rolling frequency baseline performs as well as learned adaptation.
candidates.boundary: Reception-aware gap rules, expected-reception self-supervision and AIS reception GNNs already exist. The graph study itself calls for temporal extensions. The proposed opportunity is a bounded later-period drift comparison, not first distinguishing reception from disabling.
candidates.approach: Train a compact reception model using other-vessel/background observations and time adaptation. Keep receiver changes, vessel transmission changes and traffic density as rival explanations. Satellite presence may corroborate a vessel's location, but cannot reveal shutdown intent.
candidates.data: Public GFW derived gap documentation and analysis routes exist, but raw multi-year messages with reliable receiver provenance and independent outage labels are not secured. Bernabé's large feed and the GNN study's private antenna are not assumed accessible. API eligibility is not the same as downloaded historical data.
candidates.fallback: Use an existing licensed regional track set for controlled reception-loss experiments. Such experiments test reception robustness, not real intentional disabling; without message exposure, stop the stronger topic.
candidates.resources: Estimate: CPU boosted trees/small temporal model, 16–32 GB RAM, 10–50 GB selected logs; no receiver hardware. The published two-RTX8000/100-hour GNN training is excluded.

results.title: A Systematic Review of Ship Wake Detection Methods in Satellite Imagery
results.abstract_snippet: The field of maritime surveillance is one of great strategical importance from the point of view of both civil and military applications. The growing availability of spaceborne imagery makes it a great tool for ship detection, especially when paired with information from the automatic identification system (AIS). However, small vessels can be challenging targets for spaceborne sensors without relatively high resolution. Moreover, when faced with non-cooperative targets, hull detection alone is insufficient for obtaining critical information like target speed and heading. The wakes generated by the movement of ships can be used to solve both of these issues. Several interesting solutions have been developed over the years, based on both traditional and learning-based methodologies. This review aims to provide the first thorough overview of ship wake detection solutions, highlighting the key ideas behind traditional applications, then covering more innovative applications based on deep learning (DL), to serve as a solid starting point for present and future researchers interested in the field.

results.title: Dark Ship Detection via Optical and SAR Collaboration: An Improved Multi-Feature Association Method Between Remote Sensing Images and AIS Data
results.abstract_snippet: Dark ships, vessels deliberately disabling their AIS signals, constitute a grave maritime safety hazard, with detection efforts hindered by issues like over-reliance on AIS, inadequate surveillance coverage, and significant mismatch rates. This paper proposes an improved multi-feature association method that integrates satellite remote sensing and AIS data, with a focus on oriented bounding box course estimation, to improve the detection of dark ships and enhance maritime surveillance. Firstly, the oriented bounding box object detection model (YOLOv11n-OBB) is trained to break through the limitations of horizontal bounding box orientation representation. Secondly, by integrating position, dimensions (length and width), and course characteristics, we devise a joint cost function to evaluate the combined significance of multiple features. Subsequently, an advanced JVC global optimization algorithm is employed to ensure high-precision association in dense scenes. Finally, by integrating data from Gaofen-6 (optical) and Gaofen-3B (SAR) satellites, a day-and-night collaborative monitoring framework is constructed to address the blind spots of single-sensor monitoring during night-time or adverse weather conditions. Our results indicate that the detection model demonstrates a high average precision (AP50) of 0.986 on the optical dataset and 0.903 on the SAR dataset. The association accuracy of the multi-feature association algorithm is 91.74% in optical image and AIS data matching, and 91.33% in SAR image and AIS data matching. The association rate reaches 96.03% (optical) and 74.24% (SAR), respectively. This study provides an efficient technical tool for maritime safety regulation through multi-source data fusion and algorithm innovation.

results.title: Multimodal Physics-Informed Graph Neural Diffusion for Edge Detection of AIS-Dark Illegal Fishing Vessels
results.abstract_snippet: Illegal fishing vessels that disable Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders cost coastal nations billions and contribute to ecological collapse. We present Multimodal Physics-Informed Graph Neural Diffusion, a lightweight edge artificial intelligence (AI) system that fuses Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), shore-captured Very High Frequency (VHF)/Long Range (LoRa) radio chatter, and Planet Scope optical imagery. A physics-driven Partial Differential Equation (PDE) encoder models Kelvin wake signatures, transforming noisy SAR into hydrodynamically plausible latent representations. Candidate wakes and radio emitters are treated as nodes in a dynamic graph. Graph evolution is governed by a learned reaction-diffusion process and meta-trained using fewer than twenty labeled tracks per region. A counterfactual explainer translates latent decisions into actionable overlays for maritime enforcement teams. The entire eight-bit quantized pipeline runs on a 15-watt NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, deployed aboard patrol skiffs. In a six-month deployment over 40 square kilometers (km²) in the Philippines, our system detected 87% of dark vessels, reduced false positives to 0.11 per km² per day, improved recall by 56% over the strongest SAR-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) baseline, cut wasted fuel by 34%, and produced court-admissible evidence in 100% of cases.

results.title: Ais-based event detection for offshore wind maintenance vessel operations: A validated framework
results.abstract_snippet: Enhancing the efficiency of offshore wind farm (OWF) operation and maintenance requires understanding vessel movements, turbine visit sequences, vessel–turbine interaction duration as vessel–turbine interaction durations, and transit times. However, detailed operational records are often unavailable because manual logging adds workload for operators. This study proposes an automatic identification system (AIS)-based framework for reconstructing turbine-level maintenance vessel operations from vessel trajectories and turbine coordinates. The framework combines heuristic vessel identification, geospatial filtering, and rule-based event detection to infer visited turbines, visit sequences, service timing, and vessel–turbine interaction durations from AIS data. It is developed using AIS data from maintenance operations at Horns Rev 3 in Denmark and externally validated using operator logs from a vessel operating at three German offshore wind farms: Amrumbank West, Kaskasi, and Nordsee Ost. For a representative validation day, the framework exactly reconstructed the full turbine visit sequence and achieved minute-level temporal accuracy. Across three months of validation, it achieved 100% visit-sequence accuracy, a mean Interaction-Duration MAE of 1.36 min, and a mean mission-duration error of 1.29%. The results show that AIS data can support reliable reconstruction of turbine-level offshore maintenance operations when proprietary records are unavailable, enabling improved vessel scheduling, routing, and maintenance planning.

results.title: Efficient SAR Vessel Detection for FPGA-Based On-Satellite Sensing
results.abstract_snippet: Rapid analysis of satellite imagery within minutes-to-hours of acquisition is increasingly vital for many remote sensing applications, and is an essential component for developing next-generation autonomous and distributed satellite systems. On-satellite machine learning (ML) has the potential for such rapid analysis, by overcoming latency associated with intermittent satellite connectivity to ground stations or relay satellites, but state-of-the-art models are often too large or power-hungry for on-board deployment. Vessel detection using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is a critical time-sensitive application in maritime security that exemplifies this challenge. SAR vessel detection has previously been demonstrated only by ML models that either are too large for satellite deployment, have not been developed for sufficiently low-power hardware, or have only been tested on small SAR datasets that do not sufficiently represent the difficulty of the real-world task. Here we systematically explore a suite of architectural adaptations to develop a novel YOLOv8 architecture optimized for this task and FPGA-based processing. We deploy our model on a Kria KV260 MPSoC, and show it can analyze a ~700 megapixel SAR image in less than a minute, within common satellite power constraints (<10W). Our model has detection and classification performance only ~2% and 3% lower than values from state-of-the-art GPU-based models on the largest and most diverse open SAR vessel dataset, xView3-SAR, despite being ~50 and ~2500 times more computationally efficient. This work represents a key contribution towards on-satellite ML for time-critical SAR analysis, and more autonomous, scalable satellites.1

results.title: AIS Matcher: A Precise Matching Method of SAR Imagery and AIS Vessel Data for Maritime Object Identification
results.abstract_snippet: This study proposes AIS Matcher, a precise matching methodology that integrates Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery and Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel data for enhanced maritime object identification.In conventional maritime surveillance workflows, SAR-based vessel detection and AIS-based positional information are typically processed independently, making cross-validation difficult and limiting the operational effectiveness of fused data utilization.Focusing on the complementary characteristics of the two sensors, this research presents an algorithm that matches vessel candidate regions (bounding boxes) extracted from SAR imagery with AIS trajectories through a multi-dimensional feature framework that includes spatial proximity (distance), temporal synchronization, geometric attributes (length and width), and heading direction.Unlike traditional approaches that rely solely on spatial proximity, the proposed method employs a weighted score-based matching mechanism that integrates distance, geometric similarity, and heading consistency, enabling stable candidate discrimination across diverse maritime environments.In real-world scenarios, multiple AIS signals may fall within the same SAR detection region, or some vessels may not transmit AIS at all, resulting in challenges such as multi-AIS ambiguity and missing matches.To address these issues, this study incorporates an intuitive verification interface that allows analysts to manually review uncertain cases, enhancing transparency in the matching process and enabling efficient post-processing even for large-scale datasets.Experiments conducted using commercial SAR imagery and real AIS logs collected across various sea regions demonstrate that the proposed method delivers consistent matching performance, with confirmed applicability even in high-density vessel traffic areas.The outcomes of this research offer significant potential for applications such as non-cooperative vessel tracking, illegal fishing monitoring, maritime safety management, and national security surveillance.By refining maritime situational awareness through SAR-AIS sensor fusion, AIS Matcher is expected to serve as a key component in next-generation intelligent maritime surveillance platforms.

results.title: Comparing spatial patterns of marine vessels between vessel-tracking data and satellite imagery
results.abstract_snippet: Monitoring marine use is essential to effective management but is extremely challenging, particularly where capacity and resources are limited. To overcome these limitations, satellite imagery has emerged as a promising tool for monitoring marine vessel activities that are difficult to observe through publicly available vessel-tracking data. However, the broader use of satellite imagery is hindered by the lack of a clear understanding of where and when it would bring novel information to existing vessel-tracking data. Here, we outline an analytical framework to (1) automatically detect marine vessels in optical satellite imagery using deep learning and (2) statistically contrast geospatial distributions of vessels with the vessel-tracking data. As a proof of concept, we applied our framework to the coastal regions of Peru, where vessels without the Automatic Information System (AIS) are prevalent. Quantifying differences in spatial information between disparate datasets—satellite imagery and vessel-tracking data—offers insight into the biases of each dataset and the potential for additional knowledge through data integration. Our study lays the foundation for understanding how satellite imagery can complement existing vessel-tracking data to improve marine oversight and due diligence.

results.title: Advancing Surveillance in Maritime Domain with Ship Wake Detection

venue.name: IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)

results.abstract_snippet: The detection of "dark" ships—vessels operating without Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders—is crucial for maritime security and law enforcement. Traditional methods relying on optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery face limitations, particularly for small, fast-moving vessels. The UEIKAP project, funded under the Research Projects of National Interest (PRIN) by Italian Ministry of University and Research, is developing a novel approach by focusing on ship wakes, which provide valuable information about vessel characteristics and activity. This manuscript presents a comprehensive overview of the UEIKAP project’s approach, which leverages advanced deep learning techniques (DL) and data fusion from diverse sources, including optical and SAR satellite imagery, AIS data, meteo-marine measurements, and synthetic wake models, to develop a robust ship wake detection system. The system architecture is presented, featuring specialized modules which exploit the capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Additionally, the integration of contextual environmental data is detailed, demonstrating its role in enhancing detection accuracy under varying meteo-marine conditions. Experimental results from the Venice campaign in July 2024 are presented, demonstrating the system’s ability to detect small vessel wakes in optical imagery while highlighting the dependence of SARbased detection on wind conditions. These findings emphasize the importance of environmental factors and provide critical insights for refining detection algorithms. The UEIKAP project, scheduled to conclude in late 2025, plans to show a new approach for maritime domain awareness, showing the value of ship wake detection for monitoring vessel activity and enforcing international maritime laws.

results.title: Frequency-Based Analysis of Matching Accuracy Between Satellite Radio Frequency and AIS Data for Ship Identification

venue.name: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering

results.abstract_snippet: Vessels can deactivate their Automatic Identification System (AIS) to operate undetected and potentially engage in illegal activities. To address this, satellite-based radio frequency (RF) data are increasingly being used for identifying such vessels. This study evaluates the matching accuracy among RF and AIS data based on the frequency and distance. RF data were acquired on 22 September, 25 September, and 7 December 2023. According to the frequency range, the dataset was separated into frequency-1 (3.024–3.077 GHz) and frequency-2 (9.3734–9.4249 GHz). Six distance thresholds (2 km, 3 km, 6 km, 8 km, 13 km, and 18 km) were employed for the matching process. The results depicted that the average matching rates were 95%, 92%, and 92% for the RF dataset on 22 September, 25 September, and 7 December, respectively. Additionally, the results revealed that the matching rates decreased with distance, e.g., for the RF dataset on 22 September, the average highest matching rate (47%) was found at a 2 km distance and the minimum matching rate (0.9%) was observed at an 18 km distance. Furthermore, the analysis delineated that frequency-2 consistently exceeded frequency-1, particularly at longer distances, showing a more stable trend in matching accuracy.

results.title: Maritime Environment Safety: Advanced Oil Spill Detection through AIS and Remote Sensing

venue.name: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

results.abstract_snippet: Oil spills constitute one of the most devastating environmental disasters that threaten marine ecosystems, coastal communities, and wildlife. From identification to intervention, prompt action is necessary to reduce the impact of oil spills. Traditionally used techniques for detection of oil spills involve direct visual surveillance or simple sampling which continues to be extremely costly, slow, and unsustainable for operating on a larger scale. In this scenario, AIS data, together with technologies for satellite remote sensing, are gradually becoming promising tools for detection and monitoring of oil spills in real time over vast stretches of ocean areas. This paper looks into the feasibility of combining the two types of data, namely vessel movements tracked by AIS, and satellite datasets consisting of SAR and optical imagery for detecting and assessing oil spills in marine waters. The strengths and challenges of integrating them as a way of enhancing the efficiency of oil spill detection and timeliness in the response is highlighted.

results.title: Unified Detection and Feature Extraction of Ships in Satellite Images
results.abstract_snippet: The increasing importance of maritime surveillance, particularly in monitoring dark ships, highlights the need for advanced detection models that go beyond simple ship localisation. Current approaches largely focus on either detection or feature extraction, leaving a gap in unified methods capable of providing detailed ship characteristics. This study addresses this gap by developing a unified model for ship detection and characterisation from Synthetic Aperture Radar images, estimating features such as true length, true breadth, and heading. The model is designed to detect ships of varying sizes while simultaneously estimating their characteristics, and experimental results show a high detection accuracy, with a recall of 87.7% and an F1-score of 93.5%. The model also effectively estimates ship dimensions, with mean errors of 1.4 ± 16.2 m for length and 1.5 ± 4.5 m for breadth. Estimating the heading proved challenging for smaller ships, but was accurate for larger ships. A total of 50% of the heading estimates were within 15 degrees of error. This unified approach offers practical benefits for maritime operations. It is especially useful in situations where both ship detection and detailed information are needed, such as predicting future ship positions or identifying ships.

results.title: Quasi-Tracking of Dark Ships with an AI-Based Multi-Mission Multi-Frequency Approach

venue.name: IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)

results.abstract_snippet: Maritime security faces persistent threats from illicit activities including poaching, smuggling, and human trafficking. "Dark" ships, vessels that do not transmit a valid Automatic Identification System (AIS) signal, exacerbate these challenges by evading detection. The SPECTRE project, funded by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) (with agreement n. 2023-4-E.0), addresses this issue through a multi-mission multi-frequency approach integrating data from Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, COSMO-SkyMed, and the upcoming IRIDE mission to enhance ship detection and quasi-tracking capabilities. Using state-of-the-art models based on YOLOv11 for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and on Mask R-CNN for optical data, SPECTRE combines deep learning (DL) techniques with super-resolution methods to improve detection accuracy, particularly for small vessels. A novel spatial-temporal matching module links multi-mission observations to reconstruct ship trajectories, enabling extended monitoring beyond single-satellite limitations. Preliminary results show robust performance in ship detection and trajectory reconstruction on specifically annotated data, highlighting the feasibility of the approach. While challenges such as sensor heterogeneity and environmental variability remain, SPECTRE’s iterative development process ensures adaptability. By late 2025, the project aims to deliver a comprehensive platform for real-time maritime surveillance, enhancing security and compliance in critical regions throughout the Mediterranean Sea.

results.title: BoatNet: automated small boat composition detection using deep learning on satellite imagery
results.abstract_snippet: Tracking and measuring national carbon footprints is key to achieving the ambitious goals set by the Paris Agreement on carbon emissions. According to statistics, more than 10% of global transportation carbon emissions result from shipping. However, accurate tracking of the emissions of the small boat segment is not well established. Past research looked into the role played by small boat fleets in terms of greenhouse gases, but this has relied either on high-level technological and operational assumptions or the installation of global navigation satellite system sensors to understand how this vessel class behaves. This research is undertaken mainly in relation to fishing and recreational boats. With the advent of open-access satellite imagery and its ever-increasing resolution, it can support innovative methodologies that could eventually lead to the quantification of greenhouse gas emissions. Our work used deep learning algorithms to detect small boats in three cities in the Gulf of California in Mexico. The work produced a methodology named BoatNet that can detect, measure and classify small boats with leisure boats and fishing boats even under low-resolution and blurry satellite images, achieving an accuracy of 93.9% with a precision of 74.0%. Future work should focus on attributing a boat activity to fuel consumption and operational profile to estimate small boat greenhouse gas emissions in any given region.

results.title: Automated wake detection from marine satellite imagery: lessons learned, methods, and perspectives from the UEIKAP project
results.abstract_snippet: Monitoring non-cooperative or poorly surveyed maritime traffic remains challenging when Earth Observation (EO) systems rely mainly on direct hull detection, especially for small vessels and cluttered marine scenes. This paper presents the main lessons learned from the Unveil and Explore the In-depth Knowledge of Earth Observation Data for Maritime Applications (UEIKAP) project, which investigated ship wakes as alternative, information-rich observables for vessel detection and characterization in satellite imagery. The proposed framework combines Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data for supervision and validation, meteo-marine contextual information, and synthetic wake simulations generated through numerical modeling. Deep learning (DL) segmentation models are used to detect wakes and, in SAR imagery, ship hulls. A dedicated post-processing chain then extracts wake geometry and derives pseudo-AIS variables, including course-related quantities and speed estimates from azimuth-shift effects. The results show that wake-based monitoring is technically feasible and can extend satellite-based maritime awareness beyond target localization alone. A central lesson of the project is that optical imagery currently provides the most reliable wake delineation under favorable visibility conditions, whereas SAR offers unique potential for kinematic inference but is much more sensitive to environmental forcing and acquisition geometry. The validation campaigns further show that wake detectability is strongly conditioned by meteo-marine context and vessel characteristics, making environmental awareness a key requirement for operational use. Overall, this paper presents the UEIKAP multimodal framework together with open-source Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 wake datasets, and defines the main methodological steps required to improve the robustness and operational applicability of wake-based monitoring for maritime surveillance and sea-use monitoring.

results.title: Ship Detection With SAR C-Band Satellite Images: A Systematic Review

venue.name: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing

results.abstract_snippet: Detecting and tracking ships remotely is now required in a wide range of contexts, from military security to illegal immigration control, but also management of fisheries and marine protected areas. Among the available methods, radar remote sensing is increasingly used due to its advantages of being rarely affected by cloud cover and allowing image acquisition during both day and night. The growing availability in the past decade of free Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data, such as Sentinel-1 images, enabled the widespread use of C-band images for ship detection. There is however a broad range of SAR data processing methods proposed in the literature, challenging the selection of the most appropriate one for a given application. Here, we conducted a systematic review of the literature on ship detection methods using C-band SAR data from 2015 to 2022. The review shows a partition between traditional and deep learning (DL) methods. Earlier methods were mainly based on Constant False Alarm Rate (CFAR) or polarimetry, which require limited computing resources but critically depend on ships' physical environment. Those approaches are gradually replaced by DL, due to the growth of computing capacities, the wide availability of SAR images, and the publication of DL training datasets. However, access to these computing capacities may not be easy for all users, which could become a major obstacle to their development. While both methods have the same objective, they differ both technically and in their approaches to the problem. Traditional methods mainly focus on ship size in spatial units (meters), whereas DL methods are mainly based on the number of ship pixels, regardless of image resolution. These latter methods can result in a lack of information on ship size, and therefore a lack of knowledge that could be useful to specific applications such as fisheries and protected area management.

results.title: DarkVesselNet: Multi-Modal Remote Sensing and Trajectory Reasoning for Dark Vessel Detection
results.abstract_snippet: Dark vessel detection requires fusing what vessels report through AIS with what satellites observe through radar and optical sensors. DarkVesselNet is a multi-modal remote sensing stack that combines Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, geospatial foundation model backbones, AIS trajectory reasoning, TGARD-style gap detection, and a Pi-DPM-inspired anomaly head. The repository exposes the system as a tested Python package and a public Hugging Face Space. The paper presents the sensor stack, backbone abstraction, fusion path, anomaly head, and current validation. The evidence currently available is software-grounded: tests for SAR speckle filtering, optical band ratios, Haversine distance, TGARD gap emission, sensor coregistration, backbone token shapes, and differentiable anomaly scoring.

results.title: A Novel Evaluation Metric for Unsupervised Learning in AIS-Based Maritime Anomaly Detection: MADQI
results.abstract_snippet: This paper introduces a new systematic framework for detecting anomalies in maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS) datasets. These anomalies include abnormal vessel behaviours related to speed, position jumps, time gaps, and turn angles. Although unsupervised learning algorithms such as Isolation Forest are widely used for detecting anomalous vessel movements, they often lack systematic and meaningful evaluation measures. To address this limitation, we propose a novel quality metric called Maritime Anomaly Detection Quality Index (MADQI). The prosed MADQI is a composite index designed to evaluate the anomaly detection performance of machine learning models without requiring labelled data. The proposed framework uses Haversine distance calculations to analyse AIS datasets and identify anomalies based on their spatial and behavioural characteristics. The proposed MADQI evaluation framework integrates four interconnected metrics: Anomaly Rate Consistency (ARC), Physical Plausibility Score (PPS), Score Distribution Separation (SDS), and Extreme Case Evidence (ECE). These metrics are combined through automatic normalisation using multi-chunk evaluation and adaptive scaling techniques. Experimental results on the AIS dataset show that the proposed framework achieved a MADQI score of 80.37%, demonstrating its effectiveness for unsupervised anomaly detection. In particular, the algorithm performed strongly in identifying abnormal vessel behaviour. Among the individual MADQI components, ECE and ARC achieved scores of 0.907 and 1.000, respectively, indicating excellent capability in detecting extreme anomalies and maintaining anomaly rate consistency. Overall, these results are encouraging and demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a reliable and meaningful approach for evaluating unsupervised anomaly detection in maritime AIS data.

results.title: Deep Learning based Detection of Fishing Vessels and Fishing Monitoring using Nightlight Images
results.abstract_snippet: The demand for maritime surveillance has given rise to the need for monitoring fishing vessel activities, particularly in addressing the challenge of "dark vessels" that operate without Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmission. This study presents a novel approach for detecting small-scale fishing vessels using nighttime light (NTL) imagery from the SDGSAT-1 satellite, combined with deep learning techniques to enhance fishing monitoring awareness along the western coast of India. A dual-branch YOLO11 architecture was developed to exploit both the 10-meter panchromatic and 40-meter RGB imagery from SDGSAT-1. The custom model architecture was specifically optimized for small object detection in NTL imagery, featuring parallel convolutional backbones that process both modalities before concatenation for enhanced feature extraction. The dual-branch YOLO11 model demonstrated optimal performance with a precision of 0.99, recall of 0.93, F1-score of 0.96, and mAP@50 of 0.96, significantly outperforming single-branch implementations of YOLOv5s, YOLOv8s, and standard YOLO11s architectures. When applied to the western coast of India, the model detected 31525 vessel instances across the temporal dataset spanning 2022-23. Cross-matching analysis with AIS data revealed that only 7146 (22.7%) of detected vessels had corresponding AIS transmissions, while 24379 (77.3%) were identified as potential dark vessels. Spatio-temporal analysis showed peak fishing activity during January-April, with a primary activity corridor parallel to the coastline within 50-100 km, corresponding to productive continental shelf areas. This research contributes to maritime surveillance capabilities by highlighting the effectiveness of nighttime lights satellite imagery for fishing vessel detection and provides valuable insights into fishing patterns and potential regulatory compliance issues in Indian waters.

results.title: Preliminary Work on Use of Automatic Identification System (AIS) Data for Shoaling Detection
results.abstract_snippet: This report describes a preliminary study undertaken in collaboration with the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers (USACE) to evaluate the utility of monitoring vessel traffic patterns on the Mississippi River using Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking data with the goal of providing forewarning of growing shoals in the navigation channel. Activities discussed include mapping AIS position coordinates to a more favorable data space, discovering and extracting river dredging events from AIS data, and visualizing river traffic in the months leading up to dredging events. The brief study period allowed for traffic data evaluation at two sites on the river; further study could include development of metrics and user interface concepts. Initial evaluations showed promise for providing advanced notice of shoals or other traffic disruptions and are deemed worthy of follow-up in order to develop a robust and useful system to assist with river management. The intent of this report is to share details of these initial efforts with the aim of supplying a starting point and providing guidance for researchers revisiting and expanding on this potentially valuable effort. We provide several suggestions for future research. A prerequisite for any of these approaches is access to sufficient historical shoaling and dredging data that can be used as ground truth for model development and validation. We share a data-driven method we developed to infer dredging locations, likely spurred by shoaling, that enabled preliminary progress. To progress to a highly confident predictive system, it is critical to obtain a robust historical database of actual shoaling events. This will be vital to train and test any future model which aims to use indirect observations - such as AIS navigation paths, satellite imagery, etc. - in order to predict shoals at their formative stages.

results.title: Sequential RF Fingerprinting for AIS: Rejecting Unknown Vessels and Insider MMSI Spoofs Days After Enrollment
results.abstract_snippet: Any AIS transmitter can claim any vessel's identity (MMSI), because nothing in the protocol authenticates it; only the transmitter's analog hardware reveals who is really sending. We treat AIS traffic as streams of bursts keyed by claimed MMSI and accumulate physical-layer evidence with a sequential test. Each burst is scored by its k-nearest-neighbor distance to enrolled fingerprints in the feature space of a classifier whose weights are fixed after training, calibrated into a tail probability, and accumulated by a geometric-entropy-minimization cumulative-sum (GEM-CUSUM) statistic. The same test rejects unknown transmitters when scored against all enrolled vessels, and exposes insider spoofs when scored against the claimed vessel. A threshold refreshed from genuine traffic alone keeps it at a stated false-alarm rate as fingerprints drift. On AIS in-phase/quadrature (I/Q) recordings captured over 13 days at the Istanbul Strait (Bosphorus), the detector rejects unseen vessels at least 10 days after enrollment. Evaluated over 50-burst trials with every vessel weighted equally, it reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.956 (95% confidence interval 0.913-0.989), where the best score computed from one burst at a time reaches 0.899. A threshold refreshed from the first quarter of the enrolled vessels' traffic holds 5.3% false alarms (3.0-9.2% across five independently trained encoders) at 88.8% detection. Scored against the claimed MMSI, enrolled transmitters spoofing another vessel are rejected at 0.991, a threat that open-set tests cannot see (AUROC 0.500, chance level). The lightweight Transformer GLFormer, reimplemented from its paper (no code is public) and retrained on the same data, reaches 0.652 in the same detector with its published in-phase input and 0.849 when given the same I/Q input as our encoder.

results.title: Exploring patient medication adherence and data mining methods in clinical big data: A contemporary review
results.abstract_snippet: BACKGROUND: Increasingly, patient medication adherence data are being consolidated from claims databases and electronic health records (EHRs). Such databases offer an indirect avenue to gauge medication adherence in our data-rich healthcare milieu. The surge in data accessibility, coupled with the pressing need for its conversion to actionable insights, has spotlighted data mining, with machine learning (ML) emerging as a pivotal technique. Nonadherence poses heightened health risks and escalates medical costs. This paper elucidates the synergistic interaction between medical database mining for medication adherence and the role of ML in fostering knowledge discovery. METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive review of EHR applications in the realm of medication adherence, leveraging ML techniques. We expounded on the evolution and structure of medical databases pertinent to medication adherence and harnessed both supervised and unsupervised ML paradigms to delve into adherence and its ramifications. RESULTS: Our study underscores the applications of medical databases and ML, encompassing both supervised and unsupervised learning, for medication adherence in clinical big data. Databases like SEER and NHANES, often underutilized due to their intricacies, have gained prominence. Employing ML to excavate patient medication logs from these databases facilitates adherence analysis. Such findings are pivotal for clinical decision-making, risk stratification, and scholarly pursuits, aiming to elevate healthcare quality. CONCLUSION: Advanced data mining in the era of big data has revolutionized medication adherence research, thereby enhancing patient care. Emphasizing bespoke interventions and research could herald transformative shifts in therapeutic modalities.

results.title: Scattering-Point Topology for Few-Shot Ship Classification in SAR Images

venue.name: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing

results.abstract_snippet: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) has emerged as a critical technology for detecting and classifying objects such as ships in challenging environments. However, few-shot learning remains a challenge due to the limited availability of labeled SAR data, complex radar backscatter, and variations in imaging parameters. In this paper, we propose a novel network, Scattering Point Topology for Few-Shot Ship Classification (SPT-FSC), which addresses these challenges by incorporating scattering characteristics into the network learning process through a scattering point topology (SPT) based on scattering key points. We design a topology encoding branch (TEB) through a series of operations to encode the topological information of scattering points, resulting in a scattering point topology embedding (SPTE) that improves the network's adaptability to the imaging mechanism and reduces imaging variability in SAR images. To effectively fuse the SPTE and image features extracted from a convolutional neural network (CNN), we introduce a novel mechanism called reciprocal feature fusion attention (RFFA). Furthermore, to address the limited diversity in the training data, we apply transfer learning methodologies and construct a fine-grained ship classification dataset by combining the OpenSARShip and FUSAR-Ship datasets. Our comprehensive experiments on these datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed SPT-FSC method, achieving high accuracy and robustness in few-shot ship classification tasks for SAR images, outperforming existing methods in this domain.

results.title: Ocean-aware deep learning for civilian maritime object detection and tracking in complex ocean environments: a comprehensive review
results.abstract_snippet: Reliable maritime object detection and tracking are essential for civilian ocean engineering applications, including vessel traffic monitoring, offshore infrastructure inspection, port management, marine debris surveillance, sea ice observation, hydrographic surveying, and environmental risk assessment. However, complex ocean environments present substantial challenges for automated perception systems because of dynamic sea surfaces, sea clutter, low SNRs, atmospheric interference, scale variation, occlusion, weak target signatures, and limited annotated datasets. This review examines recent advances in ocean-aware deep learning for maritime detection, segmentation, localization, and tracking using optical, infrared, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), multibeam echosounder (MBES), satellite, airborne, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), unmanned surface vehicle (USV), and autonomous sensing data, together with Automatic Identification System (AIS) information. It synthesizes methodological developments in robust feature extraction, multi-scale representation, small-object detection, multimodal data fusion, weakly supervised learning, domain adaptation, and tracking under intermittent visibility. Existing limitations remain in sea-state annotation, cross-sensor benchmarking, long-term tracking datasets, operational validation, and real-time deployment. Future research should prioritize sea-state-aware architectures, physics-informed learning, SAR–optical–AIS–MBES–USV data fusion, synthetic data generation, lightweight implementation, and standardized evaluation protocols. These directions are critical for developing reliable civilian maritime monitoring systems under diverse sensor, weather, and ocean conditions.

results.title: Spatial-Temporal Data Mining for Ocean Science: Data, Methodologies and Opportunities

venue.name: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data

results.abstract_snippet: With the rapid amassing of spatial-temporal (ST) ocean data, many spatial-temporal data mining (STDM) studies have been conducted to address various oceanic issues, including climate forecasting and disaster warning. Compared with typical ST data (e.g., traffic data), ST ocean data presents some unique characteristics, e.g., diverse regionality and high sparsity. These characteristics make it difficult to design and train STDM models on ST ocean data. To the best of our knowledge, a comprehensive survey of existing studies remains missing in the literature, which hinders not only computer scientists from identifying the research issues in ocean data mining but also ocean scientists to apply advanced STDM techniques. In this article, we provide a comprehensive survey of existing STDM studies for ocean science. Concretely, we first review the widely used ST ocean datasets and highlight their unique characteristics. Then, typical ST ocean data quality enhancement techniques are discussed. Next, we classify existing STDM studies for ocean science into four types of tasks, i.e., prediction, event detection, pattern mining, and anomaly detection, and elaborate the techniques for these tasks. Finally, promising research opportunities are discussed. This survey can help scientists from both computer science and ocean science better understand the fundamental concepts, key techniques, and open challenges of STDM for ocean science.

results.title: Deep Learning for Combating Wildlife and Environmental Crime: A Survey
results.abstract_snippet: Wildlife and Environmental Crime (WEC) describes illegal activities that threaten biodiversity and harm the environment. In recent years, deep learning (DL) has shown strong potential in combating WEC by learning complex patterns in data through the extraction of high-dimensional features. DL also offers powerful capabilities for prediction, classification, and object tracking, and has become an increasingly valuable tool in conservation efforts. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in DL implementations to combat WEC. We introduce a new taxonomy that identifies key intervention points across four contexts: field (observations in natural ecosystems); records (administrative and legal data); physical (specimens in laboratories, markets, and enforcement facilities); and online platforms. Moreover, we review existing DL-based applications for WEC prevention and discuss key opportunities, as well as the remaining challenges. Finally, we outline future research directions that may enable more robust DL-based approaches to combat WEC.

results.title: Deep Learning Methods for SAR Ship Classification under Data Scarcity, Class Imbalance, and Limited Resolution

venue.name: Electronic Theses and Dissertations Repository (University of Pisa)

results.abstract_snippet: Deep learning has become a dominant approach in processing remote sensing data, included Synthetic Aperture Radar imagery (SAR) for ship classification, yet operational deployments remain constrained by three practical factors: limited labelled datasets, long-tailed class distributions, and altered information content in SAR imaging due to noise and limited spatial resolution. The objective of this thesis is the systematic analysis of these issues, and the development of deep learning-based countermeasures aiming at the improvement of the ship classification task through the processing of SAR images, under real experimental conditions. Based on a thorough assessment of the related scientific literature, the thesis first goes through the background and taxonomy for SAR ship classification, covering the currently available datasets, the mostly exploited core architectures (convolutional and attention-based), and the many challenges potentially emerging during the model preparation phases. Building on this foundation, the analysis focuses on data scarcity, dataset quality, and domain shift. Inter-dataset generalisation has been assessed under a shared three-class setting, showing that cross-dataset performance can degrade substantially, even when label sets overlap. In addition, the sensitivity of deep learning algorithms to training objectives across datasets has been investigated, showing that the relative behaviour of loss functions can change under dataset shift. This reinforces the idea that the objective function is not a fixed default, but must be considered a critical component of the model, to be carefully adapted and optimized. This work also addresses class imbalance and training dynamics in the case of long-tailed SAR ship datasets, demonstrating that overall accuracy can remain deceptively stable while minority-class performance and stability remain poor. To counteract this, the thesis develops imbalance-aware training strategies based on curriculum learning and weighted losses, and introduces an imbalance-aware evaluation score designed to complement overall accuracy and macro-F1 in long-tailed regimes. Further analysis concerns feature-space oversampling as a representation-level alternative to naive image duplication. It is shown that enriching minority regions of the embedding space can improve minority-class recognition. Afterwards, data quality issues are considered, by studying super-resolution (SR) for SAR ship classification. First, the relationship between image fidelity improvements and downstream recognition is analysed, demonstrating that gains in common fidelity metrics do not reliably translate into improved classification performance. Motivated by this mismatch, a second approach is presented, proposing a classification-aware SR framework that aligns SR optimisation with recognition objectives through stage-wise training and loss design, supported by extensive quantitative comparisons and qualitative analyses. Overall, this thesis provides a unified view of robustness for SAR ship classification along three coupled axes: scarcity and dataset shift, imbalance and training dynamics, and pixel-level information content. The results support practical guidelines for evaluation and model design, including the use of class-sensitive metrics, cross-dataset testing when claiming robustness, imbalance-aware training strategies when long-tailed distributions dominate, and task-level validation for preprocessing interventions such as super-resolution. Together, the contributions aim to support the development of SAR ship classifiers that remain reliable when training data are scarce, heterogeneous, and imbalanced, and when the input pixel contain limited discriminative detail.
